'''''Prunus nigra''''', the '''Canada plum''',<ref name="grin">{{GRIN|accessdate=May 17, 2007}}</ref><ref name="FNA"/> '''Canadian plum''',<ref>{{PLANTS |id=PRNI |taxon=Prunus nigra |accessdate=14 October 2015}}</ref> or '''black plum''',<ref name=grin/> is a species of ''[[Prunus]]'' native to eastern North America.

==Description==
''Prunus nigra'' is a [[deciduous]] shrub or small tree growing to {{convert|10|m|abbr=off}} tall with a trunk up to {{Convert|25|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in diameter, with a low-branched, dense crown of stiff, rigid, branches. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is gray-brown, older layers coming off in thick plates. The branchlets are bright green at first, later become dark brown tinged with red, and spiny. The winter buds are chestnut brown, long-pointed at the tip, up to {{convert|8|mm|frac=8}} long.<ref name="FNA"/>

The [[leaves]] are [[Leaf shape|alternate, simple, and oblong-ovate or obovate]], {{convert|5–12|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and {{convert|3–7|cm|abbr=on|frac=8}} broad, wedge-shaped, slightly heart-shaped, or rounded at base, doubly crenaulate-serrate, abruptly contracted to a narrow point at the apex, feather-veined, midrib conspicuous; they emerge from the bud convolute, downy, slightly tinged with red, are smooth, becoming bright green above and paler beneath when full grown. The leaf [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] are stout, bearing two large dark glands and early deciduous, lanceolate, and three to five-lobed stipules.<ref name="FNA"/>

The [[flowers]] are {{convert|15–25|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} diameter, with five rounded petals, white fading to pale pink, with a more or less irregularly notched margin; they are slightly fragrant, borne in three to four-flowered [[Umbel|umbels]], with short, thick peduncles, and appear before the leaves in mid to late spring. The flower stalks are slender and dark red. The [[Sepal|calyx]] is conic, dark red, five-lobed, the lobes acute, finally reflexed, glandular, smooth on the inner surface, imbricate in bud, ovate, with short claws, imbricate in bud. There are 15–20 [[Stamen|stamens]], inserted on the calyx tube; the filaments are thread-like, the anthers purplish, introrse, and two-celled; the cells open longitudinally. The [[pistil]] has a superior ovary in the bottom of the calyx tube, being one-celled, with two ovules.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1|242341592|Prunus nigra |family=Rosaceae |first=Joseph R. |last=Rohrer}}</ref>

The [[fruit]] is an oblong-oval [[drupe]], {{convert|25–30|mm|abbr=on|frac=8}} long with a tough, thick, orange red skin, free from bloom, yellow flesh adherent to the stone; the stone oval, compressed. It matures in late summer or early autumn. The [[cotyledon]]s are thick and fleshy.<ref name="Keeler">{{cite book|author=Keeler, H. L.|year=1900|title=Our Native Trees and How to Identify Them|pages=119–122|publisher=[[Charles Scribner's Sons]]|place=New York}}</ref><ref name="FNA"/>

===Similar species===

The species can easily be confused with the related ''[[Prunus americana]]'', differing most obviously in the leaf margins having blunt, gland-tipped teeth, rather than the sharp, glandless teeth of ''P. americana'' leaves.

==Distribution and habitat==
It can be found from [[Nova Scotia]] west to [[Minnesota]] and southeastern [[Manitoba]], and south as far as [[Connecticut]], [[Illinois]], and [[Iowa]].<ref name="grin" /><ref>{{BONAP|genus=Prunus|species=nigra|date=2014}}</ref> It is [[endangered]] in [[Ohio]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Canada Plum |url=https://ohiodnr.gov/discover-and-learn/plants-trees/flowering-plants/canada-plum |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=[[Ohio Department of Natural Resources]]}}</ref> Isolated populations are present along streambanks in [[Saskatchewan]] and [[Alberta]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Sawatzky |first1=Rick |title=Plums on the Prairies |url=http://www.fruit.usask.ca/articles/plums.pdf |access-date=16 August 2016 |website=University of Saskatchewan Fruit Program}}</ref> along [[Lake Timiskaming]] in [[Northern Ontario]],<ref name="ROM">{{cite book |last1=Soper |first1=James H |url=https://archive.org/stream/shrubsofontario00sope#page/204/mode/2up |title=Shrubs of Ontario |last2=Heimburger |first2=Margaret, L |date=1982 |publisher=Royal Ontario Museum |isbn=978-0-88854-283-0 |location=Toronto |page=205}}</ref> and along the [[Maine]]-[[New Brunswick]] border.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |date=8 August 2012 |title=Green Peach Aphid |url=http://www2.gnb.ca/content/gnb/en/departments/10/agriculture/content/crops/potatoes/green_peach.html |access-date=16 August 2016 |website=New Brunswick Department of Agriculture, Aquaculture and Fisheries}}</ref>

The species grows best in [[alluvial soils]] or over [[limestone]].<ref name="nb">{{Cite web |title=Prunus nigra Ait. Canada plum - New Brunswick tree and shrub : Species of concern |url=http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca:80/subsite/mx-212/canadaplum |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20110106183810/http://cfs.nrcan.gc.ca:80/subsite/mx-212/canadaplum |archive-date=2011-01-06 |access-date=2026-09-03 |website=Natural Resources Canada |language=en}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The population along the Maine-New Brunswick border is severely threatened as the tree is a host for an [[aphid]] that menaces the local [[potato]] crop,<ref name=":0" /> with many of the trees having been cut down to reduce this problem.

A fungus in the genus ''[[Taphrina]]'' often attacks the plums; the young ovaries swell, often much larger than full grown plums, become hollow and often persist on the tree in winter. Known as "plum pockets", they appear pale green, leathery to the touch, and hollow with the exception of a few fibrous bands. The disease reduces regeneration of the plums.<ref name=nb/><ref name=Keeler/>

==Uses==
[[File:2016.04.08 19.19.14 DSC03234 - Flickr - andrey zharkikh.jpg|thumb|Cultivated specimen in bloom in Utah]]

The fruit is somewhat sour, clingstone, and very juicy. It can be eaten raw when fully ripe or cooked and made into pies, [[preserves]], and jellies.<ref name=Keeler/><ref>{{cite book|last=Little|first=Elbert L.|title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Trees: Eastern Region|publisher=Knopf|location=New York|year=1980|isbn=0-394-50760-6|page=503}}</ref> Dried, these plums were a popular winter staple of indigenous peoples. French explorer [[Jacques Cartier]] remarked in his journal that he was presented with dried Canada plums by the [[St. Lawrence Iroquoians]] in his first expedition to Canada.<ref>{{cite book|author=Carl Ortwin Sauer|year=1975|title=''Sixteenth Century North America: The Land and the People as Seen by the Europeans''|pages=80–81|publisher=University of California Press|place=Berkeley, California}}</ref>

One of the few tree fruits indigenous to the [[Upper Midwest]] of the U.S., Northern Ontario and the prairie provinces of Canada and capable of surviving the harsh winters there, efforts were made to breed improved cultivars of these plums in the 19th century.<ref name=PlumsCanada>{{cite book|author=D.S. Blair|year=1954|title=''Plums for Cold Areas of Eastern Canada''|publisher=[[Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada|Department of Agriculture]]|place=[[Ottawa]]|url=http://publications.gc.ca/collections/collection_2015/aac-aafc/A53-849-1968-eng.pdf}}</ref> Notable varieties still grown today include "Assiniboine" and "Cheney". ''P. nigra'' has the same number of chromosomes as ''[[Prunus salicina|P. salicina]]'', the cultivated Japanese plum, and so the two cross-pollinate readily.<ref>{{cite web|title=Japanese-American Hybrid Plums|url=http://uncommonfruit.cias.wisc.edu/japanese-american-hybrid-plums/|website=University of Wisconsin-Madison Center for Integrated Agricultural Systems |access-date=30 September 2016}}</ref> Breeding work in the 20th century resulted in improved ''P. nigra x salicina'' hybrid varieties that retain the high quality of Japanese plums and the hardiness of wild Canada plums, such as "Pembina", "Superior", and "Patterson Pride".<ref name=PlumsCanada />

The [[wood]] is bright red brown; heavy, hard, strong, and close-grained, with a density of 0.6918.<ref name=Keeler/> When wounded the wood turns an attractive red colour, and sawlogs of intentionally wounded trees are sought after by woodturners.{{cn|date=December 2023}}

==In culture==
The autobiographical novel ''[[On the Banks of Plum Creek]]'', the fourth book in [[Laura Ingalls Wilder]]'s ''[[Little House on the Prairie]]'' series, popularized the use of these wild plums for dried fruit by early settlers in the western U.S. and Canada.{{cn|date=December 2023}}
